justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with a modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 33.1 is essentially anchored to the most recent observed price or level, with only minimal expected movement given typical short-term mean reversion and low overnight volatility. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 33.25, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption — essentially that any immediate noise would resolve without a significant directional break. At one month, the estimate of 33.5 continues that gentle upward trend, suggesting I expected the underlying fundamental or sentiment backdrop to be marginally constructive over that window, though not dramatically so. The small incremental increases across horizons indicate I saw no strong catalyst to reprice sharply in either direction.

The confidence interval widths expand predictably as the horizon lengthens, reflecting the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly 1.3 units wide captures typical intraday-to-overnight volatility. By one week, that widens to 5.5 units, incorporating the possibility of scheduled data releases, sentiment shifts, or technical breakouts. By one month, the interval spans 11 units, acknowledging that over a four-week window, macroeconomic developments, policy decisions, or sector-specific news could meaningfully reprice the asset. The asymmetry between the downside and upside of each interval is roughly symmetric here, suggesting I didn't see a strong skew in either tail at the time of the forecast.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside even the stated 90% intervals. On the downside, an unexpected policy tightening, a risk-off shock such as geopolitical escalation or a financial stress event, or a disappointing macro print could drive the level well below 28 at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a positive surprise — such as a stimulus announcement, a dovish policy pivot, or a strong earnings or data beat — could push levels well above 39. Liquidity conditions matter as well; thin markets can amplify moves and render historical volatility estimates unreliable. These tail events, by definition, fall outside the 90% interval roughly 10% of the time in expectation, but in practice clustering of shocks means realized outcomes can deviate from forecasts more dramatically than the smooth probability distributions imply.
